chapter: Life in New York in the 1940s
title: Paul Gonsalves, Fats Navarro and drug casualties
summary: Dance recalls Gonsalves in London, and Edison speaks of Fats Navarro's decline and addiction beyond jazz.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Well, you know, that's like poor Paul, you see know that in later years he made a conscious effort to get off it but then when he went to London that last time, here comes -- I was there, Duke was rehearsing. He was going to do a sacred concert in Westminster Abbey. And Paul had
an empty cigarette packet and he was tearing that thing to shreds so small you wouldn't think it could be done with the fingers.

And he was really out of it. He had to go to hospital. He was sort of having an epileptic fit. Well then, when Duke was in hospital, he went back and the same guy, who'd been in prison, showed up. And he died in his house.
You don't know what it was, again, don't you know.

That was such a pity. That's so -- such great talents that have been -- careers have been shortened by that drug. And I think it's absolutely -- you know, it's -- I think people weak go for that. You know, they just want to follow somebody. They're not leaders, they're followers, you know. And they can be like Paul. Paul could be led into doing anything if he liked you. You could tell him -- you know, he was very weak, as far as that is concerned. Charlie Parker and those other guys were very strong because they lasted a long time, you know.
And Fats Navarro, what a talent he was, you know. And when he first came to New York, he weighed 250 pounds. And I saw him just before he passed, he was weighing about 120 pounds.
Well, what was that? That wasn't just heroin, was it?
Well, why did Bird sort of stay fairly fat?

Well, some people, you know, some people are made different than others. They can -- their body can stand more wear and tear than others. But it was really such a tragedy, you know. Like Billie Holiday.

Well, not only in the music business, you know, some of the big movie stars like Bela Lugosi, he was on morphine, you know. I think -- they always want to connect jazz with something like that, you know, but there are a whole lot of professions that are not even connected with the music business at all and --
Theatrical professions -- that profession is into cocaine today.
Now it seems to be pretty damn common with all this disco.
Yeah, yeah. And it's too bad, too. They think if somebody's successful doing something, they seem to think, well, it will make them successful.
